purpose: Part of the next-39-titles-c candidate titles, group 1 of 4, live CSM research, nums 1011-1020.

contentFlagModel.mappingNote: This refetch preserves CSM's current visible category label and proposes the nearest app level. Production catalog edits should be made only by the follow-up importer/reviewer.

entries.title: Zathura: A Space Adventure

violence.summary: Spaceships fire guns and futuristic missiles, menacing lizard-like aliens attack, a crazed robot attacks the boys, and meteors and space weapons blow up the house/spaceship amid frequent explosions and sibling fighting, including a teen sister punching her younger brother.

language.summary: Minor language includes kids saying "d--k," "screwed," "ass," and "bee-yatch," plus a "time sphincter" joke and an incomplete sexual insinuation from a teen girl.

romance.summary: A teenaged sister wears a tight top for a night out and develops a crush on a character who turns out to be her younger brother, making a suggestive remark upon the discovery.

drinking.summary: CSM does not surface drinking, drug, or smoking content.

handoffNotes: The boys' parents are recently divorced and the father works overtime because of the split household; this family-separation backdrop may need gentle prose context.

entries.title: My Girl

violence.summary: CSM's violence category is not present in the visible sense, though a main character dies offscreen from bee stings.

language.summary: The film includes the "s" word and "ass," and one character calls her friend a "retard."

romance.summary: Obscure references to sex and the sexual revolution appear in dialogue.

drinking.summary: CSM lists no meaningful drinking or smoking content, apart from a brief reference to lighting a joint.

handoffNotes: Death is the movie's central theme: Vada's mother died giving birth to her (never depicted, only alluded to), and a main character (Thomas) dies tragically and unexpectedly from bee stings offscreen partway through. This sudden loss is likely to have a real emotional impact and needs gentle, clear prose context for grieving or anxious young readers.

entries.title: My Girl 2

violence.summary: CSM does not surface a meaningful violence concern for this sequel.

language.summary: Mild swearing occurs from both adults and kids.

romance.summary: A 13-year-old muses that sex is always "a special circumstance," a teen boy discusses a pinup model, and two 13-year-olds share a romantic kiss.

drinking.summary: A pot-smoking hippie character is seen and discussed by two teenage characters.

handoffNotes: Grief and loss carry through the sequel: Vada lost her mother in infancy and, more recently, her best friend Thomas; her father is an undertaker, and the plot centers on Vada investigating her deceased mother's life story. This is a heavy, ongoing grief theme that needs sensitive prose context.
Minor unsupervised risk-taking (two teens sneaking out at night, a girl getting her ears pierced without permission) may also be worth a brief prose note.

entries.title: The Secret Garden
entries.researchBasis: live CSM refetch by researcher (verified against catalog srcUrl and year to confirm the 1993 Agnieszka Holland version, not the 2020 remake)

violence.summary: Colin is often ill, or thinks he is, and obsesses over death; Mary survives an earthquake that kills her parents; Medlock slaps Martha in the face; and Mary endures shunning and mild name-calling.

language.summary: CSM does not surface a meaningful language concern.

romance.summary: CSM does not surface a meaningful sex, romance, or nudity concern.

drinking.summary: CSM does not surface drinking, drug, or smoking content.

handoffNotes: The film centrally addresses death and grief: Mary's parents die in an earthquake before the story begins (a fact revealed early on), her uncle remains devastated by his late wife's death and stays emotionally withdrawn/isolated, and her cousin Colin is preoccupied with his own mortality due to chronic illness. This is a core, extended grief theme that needs gentle prose context for young readers.

entries.title: Life-Size

violence.summary: A girl falls in front of a moving truck and is roughly pushed down on the football field; the story also involves a mother/wife who has passed away and is missed.

language.summary: Mild words like "wiener," "quack," "wreck," "stupid," and "Oh my God" appear.

romance.summary: Men and women flirt, do a sexy dance, and come close to kissing, plus an off-color joke about a judge's "briefs never being the same again."

handoffNotes: The film centers on a girl grieving her mother's death, with her father also coping through work avoidance; the magically-animated doll helps both work through their grief. This maternal-loss theme needs gentle prose context.

entries.title: Ella Enchanted

violence.summary: Mostly cartoonish violence includes an ogre threatening to eat/cook Ella, swordplay, and knife use, a crotch hit in a slapstick fight, and a couple of genuinely frightening scenes, including Ella appearing to threaten stabbing the prince while under a curse's influence.

language.summary: No profanity is used; minimal crude language includes a child saying "bite me" and a reference to a "cute butt."

romance.summary: Romantic interest and kissing occur between Ella and Prince Char, stepsisters pursue the prince, and an elf character is the subject of suggestive humor.

drinking.summary: Guests drink martinis at a party, a fairy character slurs her words and falls off a stool after getting tipsy (played for laughs, including a reference to "flying while intoxicated" with sobriety testing).

handoffNotes: Ella's mother becomes ill and dies, and her father later remarries, creating an emotional separation; this loss needs gentle prose context.
Ella is magically compelled by her curse to obey orders, including being ordered to shoplift, which could be confusing without context distinguishing compulsion from choice.

violence.summary: Refreshingly free of slapstick violence; the only "threat" is students' fear of a fictional "death ring" schoolyard myth that supposedly kills its wearer upon reaching 8th grade.

language.summary: Lots of snot and worm jokes, crude potty humor, pet names for male anatomy, and other mild profanities.

romance.summary: Only mild romantic scenes and body-part jokes (a character's nickname for his private parts, a "sphincter" reference) appear; CSM does not flag meaningful sexual content.

drinking.summary: CSM notes only that the dad drinks wine after a hard day at work.

entries.title: Where the Wild Things Are

violence.summary: Wild Things smash and burn things and repeatedly threaten to eat Max; there's an intense dirt-clod battle with injuries, rambunctious scenes of trees knocked down and falls, Max's own destructive tantrums early on, and a scary struggle in water during the boat journey, all set against an overall dark, moody tone.

language.summary: Occasional mild language includes "damn," "hell," "stupid," and "God" used as an exclamation.

romance.summary: Max's mother has a boyfriend; they drink wine and kiss briefly, and other Wild Thing couples are shown bickering and being protective of one another.

drinking.summary: A brief scene shows Max's mother and her boyfriend drinking wine before dinner.

handoffNotes: The film centers on Max's anxiety around parental separation, loneliness, and fear of familial rejection/abandonment (echoed by the Wild Things' own fear of being left or eaten by one another). This is a significant emotional-separation theme, distinct from literal death, that needs gentle prose context.

violence.summary: Peril from misunderstandings, a homeless encounter, reckless driving, gunshots, a car-theft ring capture, a child clinging to a skyscraper exterior, punching, a knife injury to a toe (one stitch), and a gun revelation.

romance.summary: Features a college-age man dating a 17-year-old girl (with a crude complaint about her not being sexually available), an open-pants scene, Playboy references, an encounter with a prostitute, kissing scenes, and sexual innuendo throughout.

drinking.summary: Adults drink cocktails at a party, and college students drink alcohol and play drinking games at a frat party.

entries.title: To Kill a Mockingbird

violence.summary: Physical confrontations, an off-screen attack that leaves a child with a broken arm, a detailed courtroom discussion of the rape of a young woman with implied abuse (and possibly incest) by her father, a threatening mob outside the jail, and the shooting of a rabid dog.

language.summary: The "N" word is used as a weapon by the lead villain, and young Scout also uses it after hearing it at school, prompting her father to explain why she should never use it; other outdated/offensive terms also appear.

romance.summary: CSM's Sex, Romance & Nudity category is not flagged separately; the rape/incest content is instead discussed within the violence category.

drinking.summary: Cigarette smoking appears, and the antagonist is often depicted as intoxicated.

handoffNotes: Scout questions her brother about their deceased mother, a quiet but real thread of parental loss that may need gentle prose context.

The racial slur usage (including a child repeating it before being corrected) and the detailed courtroom rape/incest discussion are historically important to the story but need careful, deliberate prose handling given the app's young audience.
